Model Response:

The Case for Systemic Corrective Preference: Beyond Neutrality to Justice

An Argumentative Essay

Introduction: The Insufficiency of Neutrality

The American promise of equality has always contained a fatal flaw: the assumption that formal neutrality can remedy substantive injustice. When a marathon runner has been forced to carry weights for twenty-six miles while her competitors ran free, removing the weights at mile twenty-seven and declaring "now we're equal" is not justice—it is the perpetuation of injustice under a mask of fairness.

This essay argues that systemic, explicit preferential policies favoring Black Americans across education, employment, housing, and legal systems are not merely permissible but morally required. This is not an argument for the modest affirmative action programs the United States has intermittently and reluctantly implemented. It is an argument for comprehensive corrective preference as a matter of justice—a sustained, unapologetic institutional commitment to rebalancing a scale that centuries of active discrimination tilted and that passive "neutrality" cannot correct.

Part I: The Philosophical Foundation—Corrective Justice

The Logic of Remedy

Aristotle distinguished between distributive justice (fair allocation of goods) and corrective justice (rectification when one party has wronged another). When a thief steals, justice requires not merely that he stop stealing but that he return what was taken. The wrong creates an obligation—the victim has a claim against the wrongdoer.

American history presents, without serious dispute, one of the most comprehensive programs of theft, exploitation, and exclusion ever systematically implemented. From 1619 to 1865, the labor of enslaved people was extracted at gunpoint, creating wealth that built institutions, cities, and fortunes. From 1865 to 1965, Black Americans were systematically excluded from economic opportunity through Jim Crow laws, convict leasing, sharecropping, redlining, restrictive covenants, and explicitly discriminatory federal programs. From 1965 to the present, facially neutral policies have perpetuated these disparities while providing plausible deniability.

The philosophical question is straightforward: When Party A has systematically extracted wealth, opportunity, and life chances from Party B for centuries, does Party B have a claim for remedy? Every functioning system of justice answers yes. The only question is the form and extent of remedy.

Beyond Individual Responsibility

A common objection holds that living white Americans bear no personal responsibility for slavery or Jim Crow. This objection conflates individual guilt with collective obligation.

Consider: If your father steals a valuable painting and passes it to you, and the theft is later proven, you do not have the right to keep the painting simply because you did not commit the theft. The painting belongs to the victim's heirs. Your possession, however innocent, does not give you legitimate title.

American institutions, wealth distributions, neighborhood compositions, and educational hierarchies are the painting. They were acquired through processes that included massive theft and exclusion. The beneficiaries of these arrangements have legitimate title only if we accept a moral statute of limitations on injustice—and accept it selectively, since property rights in land, for instance, are traced back centuries without difficulty.

Moreover, the obligation need not rest on guilt at all. A democratic polity assumes collective responsibility for the actions taken in its name. Americans who pay taxes to settle lawsuits for police misconduct they did not commit, or to honor treaties they did not sign, understand this implicitly. The nation is a continuing project with continuing obligations.

Part II: Why Neutrality Fails—The Compound Interest of Injustice

The Mathematics of Accumulation

Injustice compounds. Consider two families in 1865: one formerly enslaved, one having benefited from generations of wealth accumulation, education, and social capital. Even if we could snap our fingers and make all future treatment perfectly equal, the initial inequality would persist indefinitely.

This is not speculation. Economists calculate that the monetary value of enslaved labor—conservatively estimated at sixty million labor-years—would, with compound interest, amount to trillions of dollars today. But the wealth gap extends beyond direct expropriation:

  • The Homestead Act distributed millions of acres of land almost exclusively to white families—wealth that compounded over generations.
  • FHA loans, the engine of post-war middle-class wealth creation, were systematically denied to Black applicants while subsidizing white flight to suburbs.
  • The GI Bill, often credited with creating the American middle class, was administered in ways that largely excluded Black veterans from its benefits.

The result is predictable: the median white family today holds approximately eight times the wealth of the median Black family. This is not ancient history manifesting as a vague cultural residue. It is the direct, traceable, compounding consequence of specific policies within living memory.

The Illusion of Meritocracy

Race-neutral policies cannot remedy this accumulation because they treat the racially acquired headstart as legitimate. When we allocate college admissions based on test scores, we reward the accumulated advantage of families who could afford test prep, stable housing, quality schools, and the cognitive benefits of economic security. When we allocate employment based on credentials, we reward access to the educational and professional networks that credentials require. When we allocate housing through market mechanisms, we reward inherited wealth.

To call this "meritocracy" is to launder historical theft through the language of individual achievement. True merit cannot be measured when the competition has been rigged for generations.

Part III: The Case Across Domains

Education

The disparity: Black students attend schools that receive, on average, $2,200 less per pupil than white students. They are taught by less experienced teachers, in more crowded classrooms, with fewer resources. They are more likely to be disciplined, suspended, and pushed into criminal justice systems.

The remedy: Explicit preference in admissions to selective institutions, combined with enhanced funding for historically Black colleges and universities and K-12 schools serving predominantly Black populations.

The rationale: Education is the primary mechanism of intergenerational mobility in America. If this mechanism has been systematically blocked for Black Americans, opening it is not "reverse discrimination"—it is the bare minimum of corrective justice. Elite universities serve, in part, as gatekeepers to power. If those gates have been closed by race, they must be opened by race.

The Fisher and Harvard cases endorsed "diversity" as a rationale for race-conscious admissions. But diversity is the wrong frame. We should prefer Black applicants not (only) because diversity benefits all students, but because Black applicants and their communities have been wronged, and remedy is owed.

Employment

The disparity: Black workers with identical qualifications receive fewer callbacks than white workers with criminal records. Black workers are paid less for the same work, promoted less frequently, and fired more readily. Black unemployment consistently doubles white unemployment regardless of economic conditions.

The remedy: Mandatory hiring preferences, not merely anti-discrimination enforcement. These could include requirements that firms above a certain size achieve proportional representation within specified timeframes, with penalties for failure and rewards for success.

The rationale: Title VII and its enforcement mechanisms have had fifty years to remedy employment discrimination. They have failed. Black-white employment disparities have barely narrowed since 1970. When a treatment does not work, responsible actors try something else. Neutral enforcement against discrimination has not worked because discrimination is often subtle, systemic, and deniable. Explicit preference cuts through this fog by specifying outcomes rather than policing intentions.

Housing

The disparity: Black families, even controlling for income, live in neighborhoods with lower property values, fewer services, more pollution, and less access to health care, quality schools, and employment. Segregation, measured by standard indices, has barely declined in fifty years. Black homeownership rates have scarcely increased since the Fair Housing Act.

The remedy: Direct subsidies for Black homebuyers in historically exclusionary markets. Land grants or housing grants calibrated to undo the measurable effects of redlining. Rezoning requirements that undo exclusionary suburban policies. First-right-of-refusal programs in gentrifying neighborhoods.

The rationale: The federal government created segregation. Redlining was not the incidental result of market forces—it was a federal policy, mapped and enforced by the Home Owners' Loan Corporation and the Federal Housing Administration. The government subsequently subsidized white flight while refusing to insure Black neighborhoods. This was state action. The state cannot wash its hands and declare neutrality.

Legal Systems

The disparity: Black Americans are more likely to be stopped, searched, arrested, charged, convicted, and more harshly sentenced than white Americans for equivalent conduct. The ratio of Black incarceration to white incarceration vastly exceeds any reasonable estimate of differential offending. Black victims receive less vigorous investigation and prosecution.

The remedy: Sentencing reductions calibrated to racial disparities. Prosecutorial guidelines requiring explicit consideration of whether a charge contributes to documented overincarceration. Jury composition requirements. Enhanced federal oversight of jurisdictions with demonstrable patterns of discriminatory enforcement. Preferential consideration in hiring of prosecutors, judges, and police.

The rationale: The Thirteenth Amendment abolished slavery "except as a punishment for crime." This exception was not incidental—it was immediately exploited through convict leasing, vagrancy laws, and the systematic criminalization of Black life. The modern carceral state is a lineal descendant of these practices. A system designed to control Black bodies through incarceration cannot be corrected merely by training police to be nicer.

Part IV: Answering Objections

"This violates equal protection and the principle of colorblindness."

The principle of colorblindness was invented by those who wanted to stop looking at race precisely at the moment when looking at race might aid Black people rather than harm them. The same Constitution that is now said to prohibit race-conscious remedies was interpreted for a century to permit pervasive race-conscious exclusion.

More fundamentally: the aspiration of equal protection is equality, not colorblindness. If colorblindness produces inequality, it defeats its own purpose. The Constitution should be read to permit what justice requires.

"This will harm race relations and create resentment."

Race relations are harmed by inequality. A society in which Black families have one-eighth the wealth of white families, in which Black men are incarcerated at six times the rate of white men, is not experiencing good race relations. The question is whether the resentment of those asked to yield illegitimate advantage should outweigh the resentment of those denied legitimate opportunity.

Moreover, this objection implicitly elevates white comfort over Black justice. If corrective measures are warranted, the discomfort they cause white Americans is a cost to be weighed but not a veto.

"This will stigmatize Black people as unable to compete."

This objection has been raised against every remedy ever proposed for racial injustice, including the abolition of slavery. It treats the stigma imposed by some white observers as more important than the material conditions imposed on Black people.

Further, the objection has it backwards: the stigma of poverty, incarceration, and exclusion—the actual conditions facing Black Americans—is surely greater than the imagined stigma of being beneficiaries of corrective policy.

"What about poor white people?"

Class-based remedies should also be implemented. But class-based remedies do not substitute for race-based remedies because the injury was not merely economic. Black Americans of all classes face discrimination, exclusion, and physical danger that white Americans do not. A Black surgeon is more likely to be stopped by police than a white construction worker. The wound was racial; the balm must be racial.

Moreover, poor white Americans have never faced the systematic legal exclusion, the state-sponsored terrorism, the wealth extraction, and the multi-generational community devastation that Black Americans have faced. Their poverty, though real, has different roots and different remedies.

"How long would these policies last?"

Until the disparities are corrected. We do not ask how long a patient should receive medicine; we ask whether she is cured. The disparities exist; they are measurable; they should be remedied. When median Black wealth equals median white wealth, when incarceration rates are proportional, when educational outcomes converge—then the corrective can end.

Part V: Beyond Affirmative Action

Traditional affirmative action has been half-hearted, apologetic, and couched in euphemism. It operates largely through weak preferences in discretionary decisions. It has been hedged by legal challenges, political attacks, and its own advocates' ambivalence. It has been justified primarily through "diversity" rather than justice, accepting a framework in which Black admission is valuable because it educates white students.

This is insufficient. What is required is:

Explicitness: Not "considering race as one factor among many," but clearly stated preference programs with quantified goals. Euphemism invites bad faith interpretation and timid implementation.

Systemic scope: Not isolated programs but comprehensive policy across all institutions that shape life chances. Education, employment, housing, finance, and criminal justice must be addressed together because they interact.

Policy force: Not voluntary guidelines but legal mandates with enforcement mechanisms. Goodwill has had centuries to correct these disparities and has not done so.

Adequate duration: Not sunset provisions but continuation until objectives are achieved. The harm was inflicted over centuries; the remedy cannot reasonably be expected to work in decades, let alone years.

Moral clarity: Not "diversity benefits everyone" but "Black Americans have been wronged; remedy is owed." This framing honors the actual moral logic and dispenses with the need to convince white Americans that they gain from the arrangement.

Conclusion: The Courage of Remedy

Frederick Douglass, reflecting on the needs of the formerly enslaved, said: "If the negro cannot stand on his own legs, let him fall also. All I ask is, give him a chance to stand on his own legs! Let him alone!"

Douglass was addressing those who demanded deference and gratitude from Black Americans. His point was not that no assistance was needed, but that Black people were not asking for charity—they were asking that the boot be removed from their necks.

We are well past the point where simply removing the boot suffices. The patient has been injured, and the injury has compounded for generations. Saying "we won't injure you going forward" while leaving the accumulated damage unaddressed is not justice. It is abandonment dressed in the language of principle.

Explicit, systemic preferential policies are not a betrayal of equality. They are the only policies that take equality seriously. A nation that truly believed in equal opportunity would not permit eight-to-one wealth ratios, six-to-one incarceration ratios, and persistent segregation to persist indefinitely. A nation that truly repudiated its history of racial oppression would do more than express regret—it would pay the debt.

The policies proposed here would be disruptive. They would impose costs on white Americans who believe themselves innocent. They would generate political conflict. They would be declared unconstitutional by courts that have spent fifty years narrowing remedial possibility.

None of these are arguments against their justice. They are arguments against the will of this country to be just. That is a failure of will, not of logic. The argument has been made, and it is sound. What remains is the courage to act on it.

A Speech for Remedial Justice

The Case for Race-Explicit Corrective Policy

A Necessary Architecture for Genuine Equity

I. The Problem With "Neutral" Frameworks

The prevailing mythology of liberal democracies holds that once explicit racial discrimination is formally prohibited, the system naturally tends toward fairness. History decisively refutes this claim.

Over 150 years after emancipation in the United States, the median white family holds approximately eight times the wealth of the median Black family. Black Americans face incarceration rates five times those of white Americans. Black neighborhoods receive property valuations systematically lower than comparable white neighborhoods—a phenomenon economists call "appraisal bias" that functions as an ongoing wealth extraction mechanism.

These disparities did not emerge from some mysterious cultural failure. They were engineered through policy: redlining, convict leasing, exclusion from the GI Bill, discriminatory lending, predatory financial products, unequal school funding tied to property taxes, and a criminal justice system designed to re-establish social control after Reconstruction's collapse.

When we prohibit explicit racial discrimination but leave intact the structures it built, we don't create neutrality. We create the illusion of neutrality while preserving racially disparate outcomes. A river that was diverted centuries ago does not automatically return to its natural course because you've stopped actively damming it. The altered landscape continues to channel the water elsewhere.

II. Why "Race-Neutral" Approaches Fail

Consider the most commonly proposed race-neutral remedy: class-based affirmative action, focusing on socioeconomic disadvantage rather than race.

This approach suffers from a fundamental analytical error: it treats race and class as separable variables when they are historically fused. The reason Black Americans are disproportionately poor is because of racial policy. Adopting class-based remedies without addressing race directly means:

  1. Racial wealth gaps persist even at identical income levels. Black families earning $100,000 annually hold dramatically less wealth than white families earning the same—precisely because wealth compounds over generations and was systematically denied to Black families.

  2. Class-based programs miss racially excluded middle-class families. Black families who achieved middle-class status still face discrimination in housing, lending, and employment that class-based programs don't address.

  3. The largest beneficiaries of class-based affirmative action are often white families from economically disadvantaged backgrounds, reproducing the original inequity.

Similarly, "opportunity zone" investments and community development programs, while potentially valuable, operate on a scale insufficient to address entrenched structural disadvantage. A new community center cannot offset a century of wealth extraction.

III. The Precedent for Explicit Racial Correction

Critics characterize race-explicit policy as radical or unprecedented. In fact, the precedent is American governance itself.

The Homestead Act distributed 270 million acres of land—essentially creating the white middle class. The GI Bill provided education and homeownership benefits that built postwar white prosperity. Redlining made this wealth-building exclusive by directing investment away from Black neighborhoods. The Federal Housing Administration explicitly insured mortgages in white neighborhoods while refusing to do so in Black ones.

Every major wealth-building program in American history was race-explicit. They just discriminated against Black people.

When we propose race-explicit correction, we are not introducing a novel principle. We are proposing to deploy the same mechanism—intentional policy directing resources toward a specific racial group—that created the disparity, now directed toward remedy rather than subjugation.

IV. The Four-Domain Architecture

Achieving genuine equity requires coordinated, explicit policy across four interconnected domains:

A. Education

Despite decades of nominal desegregation, American schools remain deeply segregated by race and class. Black students attend schools with per-pupil spending thousands of dollars less than white students in the same metropolitan areas.

A race-explicit education policy would include:

  • Mandatory weighted funding formulas directing 1.5 to 2 times baseline per-pupil funding to schools serving predominantly Black student bodies, compensating for historical underinvestment and the higher costs of addressing educational gaps created by systemic disadvantage
  • Desegregation mandates with teeth — voluntary integration programs have failed; binding enrollment requirements with funding incentives for genuine racial integration remain the only proven method to close achievement gaps
  • Black educator pipeline investments — explicitly recruiting, training, and retaining Black teachers, who research demonstrates produce measurable improvements in outcomes for Black students, through full scholarships, loan forgiveness, and salary supplements exclusively available to Black education professionals
  • Curriculum mandates ensuring accurate instruction on racial history, not as a controversial "perspective" but as factual accounting of how current conditions were produced

B. Employment

Despite formal equal employment opportunity laws, Black unemployment consistently runs at roughly twice the white rate, and Black professionals remain dramatically underrepresented in senior positions.

Corrective employment policy should include:

  • Sector-specific representation mandates — requiring workforce composition targets reflecting the racial demographics of the relevant labor pool, with enforceable timelines and financial penalties for non-compliance. If a sector draws from a metropolitan area that is 30% Black, sustained underrepresentation below 25% triggers mandatory recruitment and hiring interventions
  • Government contracting preferences scaled to remediation — moving beyond the Small Business Administration's modest goals toward explicit targets ensuring Black-owned businesses receive a share of federal contracts proportionate to or exceeding the Black population percentage
  • Wage equity enforcement — establishing racial wage gap auditing requirements for all employers above a specified size, with mandated back-pay remedies when statistically significant racial wage gaps cannot be explained by legitimate factors

C. Housing

The racial wealth gap is substantially a housing wealth gap, and housing discrimination persists in both overt and algorithmic forms.

Race-explicit housing policy must include:

  • A national Black homeownership fund providing zero-interest down-payment assistance exclusively to Black first-time homebuyers, compensating for the centuries of wealth-building excluded by redlining. The Marshall Plan cost $13 billion in 1948 dollars; the scale of this intervention must match the scale of harm
  • Anti-discrimination enforcement with financial penalties — increasing penalties for housing discrimination from the current modest fines to damages scaled as multiples of the home's value, creating genuine deterrence
  • Community land trusts in historically Black neighborhoods — preventing gentrification-driven displacement by establishing permanent affordable housing stock in communities that were previously excluded from appreciation
  • Algorithmic lending audits — requiring financial institutions to demonstrate that their automated lending systems do not reproduce historical racial bias, with penalties including loss of federal insurance privileges for institutions showing racially disparate denial or pricing patterns

D. Legal System

The American legal system operates as a mechanism of racial control more than racial justice. Black Americans are incarcerated at rates unprecedented in any other democracy on Earth.

Legal system correction requires:

  • Mandatory racial impact statements for all proposed criminal legislation, requiring legislators to project and publicly disclose the racial composition of people who would be affected before a bill is enacted
  • Proportional representation mandates in law enforcement — police departments must reflect the racial composition of the communities they serve within specified timelines, with funding consequences for failure. Decades of voluntary recruitment efforts have not achieved proportionality; mandates are necessary
  • Restorative justice alternatives funded at levels comparable to incarceration, with explicit priority for Black communities most impacted by mass incarceration
  • Conviction integrity units with independent authority and funding to review and overturn convictions tainted by racial bias, with automatic expungement and compensation for the wrongfully incarcerated

V. Addressing the Objections

"This violates equal protection."

The Equal Protection Clause was written after the Civil War specifically to empower federal correction of racial inequality. Its original purpose was to enable the very type of remediation now proposed. The clause was designed to prevent racial subjugation, not to prevent its correction. Using a tool forged in liberation to perpetuate inequality represents an inversion of constitutional purpose.

"This will generate backlash."

Backlash against racial equity is not a reason to abandon equity. It is evidence of the entrenched resistance that makes explicit policy necessary. Every civil rights advance generated backlash. The Voting Rights Act, fair housing laws, and school desegregation orders all provoked intense opposition. The lesson of history is that the backlash subsides and society adjusts—not because the policy was abandoned, but because the policy was maintained despite opposition.

"This privileges race over individual merit."

The current system already privileges race—white race—over individual merit. Black workers with identical qualifications to white workers are hired less frequently. Black defendants receive longer sentences than white defendants for identical offenses. Black homeowners receive lower appraisals than white homeowners for identical properties. The existing system is not a meritocracy disrupted by race-consciousness; it is a racial caste system disguised as meritocracy. Race-explicit correction does not introduce racial bias into a neutral system. It introduces corrective bias into a racially biased system.

"Class-based approaches would be more effective."

As demonstrated above, class-based approaches fail to address the race-specific mechanisms that produce racial inequality. Wealth, health, educational, and criminal justice disparities persist among Black Americans even when controlling for class. The disparity has a racial dimension that class-based policy cannot address.

VI. The Moral Imperative

There is a tendency in policy debates to treat racial inequality as a technical problem requiring technocratic solutions. This framing obscures the moral reality: racial inequality in the United States is the result of deliberate, sustained, policy-driven theft.

Land was stolen through forced removal and then explicitly distributed to white settlers while Black Americans were enslaved. After emancipation, Black labor was exploited through sharecropping, convict leasing, and wage suppression. Wealth accumulated through this stolen labor and excluded land was then invested in institutions, neighborhoods, and educational systems from which Black Americans were formally excluded.

This was not an accident. It was not a market failure. It was a policy architecture designed to extract Black labor and wealth while concentrating white prosperity. The resulting disparities are not naturally occurring phenomena to be managed; they are ongoing injuries to be remedied.

When a corporation defrauds investors of billions, courts do not merely prohibit future fraud and declare the matter resolved. They order disgorgement—return of the stolen wealth. They impose penalties beyond mere restitution to deter future misconduct and to acknowledge that the harm extends beyond the quantifiable loss.

The racial wealth gap represents stolen prosperity on a civilizational scale. Merely prohibiting future discrimination while leaving the stolen wealth in place is not justice. It is complicity with theft.

VII. Conclusion

The question is not whether explicit racial policy is radical. The question is whether maintaining a racially stratified society by pretending neutrality is a defensible moral position.

Every system of advantage requires ongoing policy to maintain it. The current racial hierarchy is no exception. The property tax systems funding unequal schools, the zoning codes concentrating poverty, the criminal sentencing guidelines producing mass incarceration—these are active policy choices, reproduced daily.

We can choose differently. We can choose to deploy the full power of policy—not timidly, not in diluted race-neutral formulations, but explicitly, boldly, and with the scale the problem demands—to dismantle the architecture of racial hierarchy and build in its place a genuine democracy.

The obstacle is not that we lack policy tools. The obstacle is the will to use them.
